Eric has been called a "guitar god" and rightly so. He was such a great example of the influence of the blues artists before him that birthed rock. With the English known to have being rather reserved and staid, it's little wonder how exciting the Blues must have been to the young artists of the time. Openly expressing deep emotions wasn't a forte in their historical musical lexicon, and I believe they welcomed a genre that allowed the freedom to explore that. Eric, and his contemporaries, grabbed that with a passion and thankfully so. Adding their enthusiasm greatly advanced a new direction in musical expression. My personal favorite period of Eric's were his earlier years, a prime example captured at Winterland in Creams 1968 live recording of Crossroads, itself a new vision of a great Blues standard. The "competition" and influence of Page, Beck, et al, of that time period helped spur the inventiveness and exploration that gave us so much great music.

I do have to say I was disappointed a few years ago to see Eric in concert, especially given my anticipation. He plainly was just calling it in and doing a tour to make some money. He was lackluster, sitting most of the concert, and didn't engage the audience or really show much interest. But I do understand why. He's played all over the world to massive audience for ~50 years. I'm not in a major market and and should be happy he even came here. Maybe because of his early performances, as I already said were my favorite period, and him being much older I was expecting too much. I certainly don't hold it against his known expertise and influence on the history of rock. He does truly deserve his place in the pantheon of "Guitar Gods".

As you probably know, today is the birthday of Sam 'Lightnin' Hopkins. He, along with his fellow early Blues artists, were never known for exceptional guitar skills. But their style of expression was unmistakably the basis for rock and the major impetus for so much music since. I might suggest an article on the more notable group of these early pioneers and how/why they were such an important part of contemporary music history. It wouldn't exactly fit into the basis of these articles, maybe as a side venture at some time.

Again, thanks. Keep up the great work.
